about_blocks.text: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre: Early Recovery for Men in Kitamaat Village
about_blocks.html: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre: Early Recovery for Men in Kitamaat Village

about_blocks.text: Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre Society is a non-profit residential addiction treatment centre in Kitamaat Village, on the traditional unceded territory of the Haisla Nation on BC's northwest coast. Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab means healing each other in the x̄á’isla language. The centre runs one program, the Early Recovery and Stabilization Addictions Program, for adult men 19 and older.

about_blocks.text: The program is built for the start of recovery. It accepts men who are still "wet" and in minor withdrawal, men on methadone or Suboxone, and mandated clients, which removes some of the barriers other programs set. The centre focuses on the first two years of recovery and says it meets people where they are, whether they are still thinking about change or already making it.

about_blocks.text: It is a small program: 13 beds, 8 funded through the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program (NNADAP) and 5 funded by Northern Health. Men can stay for a full 6, 7, 8 or 12-week cycle, come for 1 to 8 modules, or attend as day patients. In 2026 the centre is running five intakes, with graduations on Wednesdays so that men who rely on public transit have two days to travel home.

about_blocks.text: Week by week, the 8-week program moves from stabilization and self-assessment to family systems, the bio-psycho-social side of addiction, post-acute withdrawal (PAWS), spirituality, healthy living and, at the end, planning for home. Alongside the groups there is alcohol and drug counselling, mental health counselling, Elder support, ceremony, yoga and mindfulness, gambling awareness, diabetes and health sessions and employment readiness. A naturopathic physician helps with withdrawal symptoms, chronic pain and lifestyle planning.

about_blocks.text: The centre achieved full accreditation through Accreditation Canada in November 2013 and belongs to the Association of BC First Nations Treatment Programs. Admission is by referral package, completed with a referral worker and a physician, and a panel of three counsellors reviews each file. Call 250-639-9817 or email intake@gyawatlaab.ca to ask about the next intake.

centre.faq_heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre

faqs.question: Who can attend Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab Healing Centre?

answer_blocks.text: The program is for adult men aged 19 and older who are in early recovery from substance use. The centre says participants come from both Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities, and each admission is assessed on its own to make sure the program is a safe fit. It welcomes mandated clients and men with addiction-related convictions, except sexual assault convictions, and takes no more than 3 clients with parole, probation or bail orders per intake.
answer_blocks.html: The program is for adult men aged 19 and older who are in early recovery from substance use. The centre says participants come from both Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities, and each admission is assessed on its own to make sure the program is a safe fit. It welcomes mandated clients and men with addiction-related convictions, except sexual assault convictions, and takes no more than 3 clients with parole, probation or bail orders per intake.

faqs.question: What type of treatment does the centre offer?

answer_blocks.text: It runs one residential program, the Early Recovery and Stabilization Addictions Program, for men in the first stage of recovery. The program is modular: you can stay for a full 6, 7, 8 or 12-week cycle, stay for 1 to 8 modules, or attend as a day patient. It mixes alcohol and drug counselling, mental health counselling, psychoeducational groups and cultural practices with support from a naturopathic physician.

faqs.question: How long is the program, and when are the intakes?

answer_blocks.text: Cycles run 6, 7, 8 or 12 weeks. The centre lists five intakes for 2026: a 12-week program from January 5, 7-week programs from April 6 and October 19, and 8-week programs from May 25 and August 17. Graduations are on Wednesdays at 2 pm so men travelling by public transit have Thursday and Friday to get home.

faqs.question: How much does it cost, and how is it funded?

answer_blocks.text: The centre does not publish a fee. Its website says it runs 8 beds funded through the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program (NNADAP) and 5 beds funded by Northern Health. The referral package it posts is the shared package for FNHA-funded treatment centres, and it asks that funding (for example corrections, an employer, FNHA, yourself or your band) and travel funding be in place before you attend. Ask the intake worker what applies to you.

faqs.question: Does Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab offer detox?

answer_blocks.text: It is not a medical detox centre, but it does accept men who are still "wet" and in minor withdrawal from their drug of choice. A naturopathic physician on the care team helps with withdrawal support, and the centre says it can request detox if staff feel it is needed.

faqs.question: Can I attend if I am on methadone or Suboxone?

answer_blocks.text: Yes. The centre welcomes people on opioid agonist treatment, including methadone and Suboxone, and lists methadone maintenance clients as eligible. Bring your prescription details into the intake package so the medical section is complete.

answer_blocks.text: Start by finding a referral worker or counsellor who will support you before and after treatment, then complete the intake package together. You also need a medical exam and a TB test, with your physician filling in the medical section, and the package goes to the centre by fax or email. A review panel of three program counsellors decides on fit, and the cut-off is 2 Wednesdays at 2 pm before the intake date.

faqs.question: Is culture part of the program?

answer_blocks.text: Yes. Elders are on staff, and the centre says cultural and spiritual practices, including traditional ceremonies and spiritual teachings, run through the program. It also says cultural approaches are offered alongside clinical care and are guided by respect and individual choice. The name Gya’ Wa’ Tlaab means healing each other in the x̄á’isla language.

faqs.question: Where is the centre and how do I get there?

answer_blocks.text: The centre is at 322H Haisla Ave in Kitamaat Village, on Haisla Nation territory at the head of Douglas Channel, a short drive from Kitimat. From Vancouver it is about 16 hours by road, so most people fly to the Northwest Regional Airport in Terrace, about an hour's drive away. Terrace is the nearest larger town and Prince Rupert is about 2.5 hours away.
